strength: It spots that the top 5 matte shades run out about 30 November even though the line shows 8 weeks of cover, then fixes it with re-cartoning, a rush order and a standard order inside ₹1.2 crore, and the maths checks out.
mistake: The glitter palette is bundled with kohl instead of the top lipsticks. The 4-per-shade cap also sits awkwardly with pros like Farah, who buy 6 to 10, although the pro pre-order softens this.
to10: Pair the glitter palette with the top lipsticks as a gift or add-on, and show the shade-level cover check for foundation and kohl rather than assuming it.

strength: It gives a date-by-date stock table for the top 5 shades with the sale planned at 2.5 times a normal week. It holds back cash to rush any foundation or kohl shade under 8 weeks, and it sets clear January decision rules with an owner for every task.
mistake: There are small date slips (held stock back on 18 Nov in one place and 19 Nov in another), and the restock message is a little flatter in our voice than it could be.
to10: Tighten the copy so it lands well under 900 words, fix the date mismatch, and give the back-in-stock line more of our bold voice.

strength: Every line has a call against the 2.5 break-even. Exact negatives kill the three losing pockets, and the forecast math (non-brand +$41,400, total $217,208) checks out, with a downside case and a Black Friday break-even reset I hadn't thought of.
mistake: It commits only $122,000 and parks $118,000 in reserve. That gives up about $114,000 of non-brand sales, and it never builds a dedicated home for the winning washable and work-comfort searches. The feed fix also skips how to stop price mismatches coming back.
to10: Put part of the reserve into a non-brand Search campaign on the winning themes, add a root-cause check and automatic item updates to the feed fix, and get Claire's 'stand all day' wording into the title.

strength: The feed fix is the most practical part: compare feed, page and structured-data prices, use sale_price with dates, turn on automatic item updates. It also adds a non-brand Search campaign and ad copy that use Claire's and Nina's own words.
mistake: It leaves $128,000 in a brand-excluded PMax that currently runs at 2.03, adds no negatives for 'women's flats' or 'sustainable shoes', and banks profit on PMax hitting 2.6 even though its best themes are moving to Search. The cautious case keeps spending at 2.2, below break-even.
to10: Block the broad and sustainable terms in PMax, cut its budget to what the proven themes support, and stop spend in any line whose cautious case falls below 2.5.

strength: Tight, correct working: it discounts the fit-finder gap for self-selection, runs the portal as a 50/50 test with a guardrail, and notes that returns lag orders.
mistake: There is no day-3 'nearly there' update and the forecasts are single numbers, not an honest range. The post-delivery fit email gives no real fit help for bra buyers.
to10: Add a day-3 update, practical fit tips in the bra post-delivery message, and low and high ranges for each saving.

strength: It covers every lever I hoped for: a dispatch email when the parcel leaves us, a day-3 update, practical bra fit tips at delivery, a swap-first portal for size reasons that keeps refund one tap away, and ranged savings with the working.
mistake: 'We're packing your order now' and 'switch for free in the next 2 hours' promise things the warehouse may not deliver. The swap count ignores the smaller return base after the fit fixes.
to10: Soften the confirmation wording so it promises nothing we can't keep, and add a guardrail metric and a note on how returns lag orders to the tracking plan.

strength: A tight one-screen flow that splits each reason by plan type and reminder status, with warm copy in our voice and a 10% holdout to test the assumed rates.
mistake: It keeps 50% off for switchers even though 61% leave when the discount ends, and it labels the switcher revenue 'after discount' while counting them at full £9.
to10: Drop the switcher discount, give an honest range showing that the pause is proven and the other rows are guesses, and set kill criteria for the untested offers.

strength: It cuts discounts entirely, puts the proven pause first, and is honest about which numbers are solid. It also gives a clear measurement plan with kill thresholds and a pre-launch checklist the team can act on.
mistake: The heading 'Before you go' leans slightly toward a retention script. It also states an unverified UK rule date and offers no holdout to prove lift.
to10: Add a holdout group to measure true lift, give the switching-apps group something more useful than a thank-you, and warm up the heading.

strength: The ranking is built on tickets we can remove, and the forecast has a clear range (1,455 to 3,395) with transparent working, plus a list of things to check before publishing.
mistake: It leaves 'How balances work' as it is, the 38%-helpful article that 21,000 people read, and bolts a new one beside it. The forecast also uses a borrowed 58% help rate that has no link to each topic.
to10: Rewrite 'How balances work' itself so Simplify debts is answered in its first lines, and set the help rate for each topic from that topic's own evidence rather than a median.

strength: It rewrites the articles people already land on, using their search words. It covers app and web restore and Pro cancellation, and it reasons through each topic, counting only the 2,000 app-store billing tickets.
mistake: The 3,700 forecast leans optimistic, and the low end is only mentioned after the point estimate. It also suggests merging an article that is already 71% helpful, and the 'Balances are simplified. Why?' line is extra engineering work on top of the one day.
to10: Lead with an explicit low-to-high range, drop the payment-article merge, and keep the in-app work inside the engineer's one day.

strength: It refuses the 20% cut with the right lifetime maths ($1,677 vs $1,130, net $1,174) and the 12.5% break-even, then sets the 90-day window and faster payouts at the heart of the plan.
mistake: Adding 40% first-year commission for Partners plus a 90-day window for everyone raises cost on top of the base, against the aim of rewarding the top 20 without lifting cost across the board, and the 30-day plan has no real dates or owners.
to10: Drop the 40% tier in favour of non-rate perks, put calendar dates and owners on the first 30 days, and model what cutting only new customers would actually save.

strength: It shows the honest saving from cutting only new customers is about $38,000, not $210,000, which ends the finance debate, and it holds 30% while fixing the window, minimum and payout speed exactly where the survey points.
mistake: The 60-day window for ordinary members still leaves part of the 41-day-median tail uncredited, and its cost isn't sized in dollars the way the other numbers are.
to10: Estimate the dollar cost of the 60/90-day windows and show what payout-fee and perk spend returns in referred revenue.

strength: Finds the top-5 stock-out and fixes it with a rush order, a standard order and re-cartoning, all inside cash (₹1,14,13,400, arithmetic checks) with ₹5.87 lakh held back. It also unloads the glitter palettes through a lipstick add-on and a dated clearance rule.
mistake: It hands the ops lead conditional homework (move foundation or kohl shades under 8 weeks to rush, a January rule that depends on sales, a liquidator decision) when the owner asked for one plan, and its date-by-date stock table is hard to follow.
to10: Remove the conditionals, give one dated action table and a full back-in-stock message in the brand voice, and trim to 900 words.

strength: A decisive plan with a clean PO table (₹1.187 crore, arithmetic checks), a cover and ending-stock table that shows why each line gets what it gets, and a dated action list the ops lead can run from Monday.
mistake: Bundling glitter palettes with kohl uses a line that is itself tight on stock. The 4-per-shade cap also sits awkwardly with bridal artists who buy 6 to 10 units, and it leaves only about ₹1.3 lakh spare.
to10: Pair the palette with the slow-moving lipsticks instead of kohl, exempt pre-booked artists from the cap, and keep a larger cash buffer.

strength: A clean profit table against the 2.5 break-even, a split that adds to $240,000, a day-by-day first week with daily budgets, and ready search headlines and title patterns in the brand's voice.
mistake: The forecast is optimistic and untested: PMax is assumed to jump from 2.0 to 2.6 and a brand-new non-brand Search campaign to earn 3.2. Brand sales are assumed to hold at 95% after the exclusion, with no way to check that, and the reserve is only $30,000.
to10: Add explicit negatives or caps for the losing 'women's flats' and 'sustainable shoes' spend, a way to check brand sales after the exclusion, clear weekly rules for weeks 2 to 4, and a more cautious forecast.

strength: It breaks the 4.0 ROAS down line by line against break-even, and it is correct on the numbers. It adds disciplined rules: a Friday reserve-release rule, a brand-exclusion test read on 14 December against Shopify new-customer orders, a Black Friday discount warning, and an owner and 'done when' for every first-week action.
mistake: Only $122,000 is committed and $118,000 sits in a rule-based reserve, so the split is less decisive. The profit forecast counts committed spend only, so what happens if the reserve is released is not modelled.
to10: Model the profit if the reserve is released, and add ready-to-paste search headlines or ad copy in the Rothy's voice.

strength: The numbers are worked step by step and all check out. It also builds in a 50/50 portal test and a 10% holdout, and it admits that fit-finder users chose the quiz themselves by closing only half the 19-point gap.
mistake: It gives single-point estimates (tickets halved, 35% swap share) instead of an honest range. It has no short day-3 'still on track' nudge and no fit guidance for first-time bra buyers after delivery, only a generic 'swap my size' email.
to10: Show low and high ranges, add a day-3 status message, and put real how-to-check-your-fit guidance in the post-delivery bra email.

strength: It opens with the cost of the problem (£139,800 in returns, £31,360 in tickets) and gives low-to-high ranges for every lever. It also covers every message the owner hoped for, including a day-3 update and a bra-specific fit-check email after delivery.
mistake: The swap-first headline of 'up to £183,800 in sales kept' is a loose upper bound. The portal pre-selects swap for size reasons, which edges toward a nudge, and it has no explicit portal A/B test.
to10: Add a controlled test of the new portal against the old one, and use a firmer, more cautious figure for sales kept.

strength: A disciplined flow with no discounts, the pause brought back for 'no time', and full copy for every reason. The money is worked through honestly (+1,329 kept, about +£10,700 a month) and the answer says the pause is the only well-supported row.
mistake: It runs well past the 1,000-word limit, and it gives the team a pre-launch checklist and a metrics list but no build order or holdout test to prove the lift.
to10: Cut it to the word limit and add a build order plus a holdout group to show the lift against today's flow.

strength: It restores the pause as the main save (79% of the subscribers kept). It adds build notes and a 10% holdout for 8 weeks, which is the right way to prove the lift. It also adds a fresh 'smaller daily goal' option for learners who already have a reminder.
mistake: It keeps a 50% discount for app switchers on an untested 3.5% guess, and the £607 for that group is counted at full price although labelled 'after discount'.
to10: Drop the switcher discount, or label it clearly as a test, and add the first-month metrics with target numbers.

strength: It finds all three signals (Simplify debts, the delete searches, the Apple and Google refunds), writes all three articles answer-first, and also covers the currency gap and the in-app links.
mistake: The forecast rests on unsupported 'share avoided' guesses (40%, 40%, 50%) and lands on a confident 3,700-ticket, 21% drop. The 50% for Pro refunds is optimistic, and the low case is just half of the same guesses.
to10: Build the forecast from a stated reach and a help rate the data supports, give a proper range up front, and trim the extras (merge, edit steps) to fit the word limit.

strength: The ticket forecast shows its working (8,361 tickets × 50% reach × 58% help rate = 2,425, about $9,900), gives a range of 1,500 to 3,400, and the number is stated at the top.
mistake: It leaves the high-view, 38%-helpful 'How balances work' article in place with only two added lines, and the 58% help rate applied to new articles is a borrowed proxy. The whole response also runs over the 1,200-word limit.
to10: Cut length to fit 1,200 words, rewrite the main balances article itself rather than only linking to it, and justify the reach figure from the data.

strength: It answers the 20% question straight, with the lifetime maths ($1,677 vs $1,130, net $1,174). It adds a break-even test (a 12.5% revenue loss, or four top partners) and a calendar-dated 30-day plan with owners.
mistake: It is probably a little over the 1,100-word limit, and it names the cost of the wider credit window as 'the cost to watch' without putting a dollar figure on it.
to10: Cut it to the word limit and give the 60/90-day window a dollar estimate, instead of leaving it as 'the cost to watch'.

strength: It gives a straight no on the cut, with the lifetime maths and break-even. It also puts dollar figures on the costs of its own proposals ($46k Partner rate, $63k per 10% window rise, $52.5k payout timing).
mistake: The payout fix is weak: 30 days after month end with a $50 minimum, when payouts were the top complaint. The plan runs on 'Days 1-7' labels, not dates, and it plans to recruit 30 more creators beyond the top 20.
to10: Fix payouts more boldly (a lower minimum and a faster schedule for everyone), use calendar dates in the first 30 days, and show how the $46k Partner-rate cost sits alongside the $40k perk budget.

strength: It finds that the top 5 shades run out around 30 November and spends the cash on a rush order plus a standard order for them. The total is ₹1.187 crore, inside the budget, and no slow line gets an order.
mistake: It counts the 3,900 held units inside the 9,100 rather than as extra stock, which hides how much the re-carton job helps. The 4-per-shade cap also works against bridal artists who buy 6 to 10 units.
to10: Count the re-cartoned units as added stock and show the top 5 shades week by week, so the gap and the order sizes are traced through the sale.

strength: A date-by-date stock table for the top 5 shades shows the pre-order gap, the sale at 2.5 times a normal week and the restock. Each task has a named owner, and there is a costed fallback for foundation and kohl inside the held-back cash.
mistake: Like the other plan, it treats the held units as part of the 9,100 rather than as extra stock, and the January rule and liquidation floor are a little vague.
to10: Count the re-cartoned units as extra top-5 stock and set a firm clearance price for the glitter palettes.

strength: It breaks the 4.0 ROAS down line by line against the 2.5 break-even, shows contribution after ads for each line, and ties the new $240,000 split to Friday reserve rules, dated first-week owners and a Black Friday freeze and discount warning.
mistake: It cuts broad 'women's flats' and 'sustainable shoes' only with exact-match negatives, which leaves most of that losing broad traffic running. It also holds $118,000 in reserve, which may underspend the month.
to10: Use a stronger way to cut the broad and sustainable themes (theme-level or phrase exclusions, or a separate non-brand Search campaign), and put the customers' own words into ad assets as well as titles.

strength: The price-mismatch diagnosis is practical and prevents a repeat: it checks the feed against the page and structured data, uses sale_price with dates, and turns on automatic item updates. It adds a non-brand Search campaign and writes ad copy in Claire's own words.
mistake: It keeps $128,000 in Performance Max without explicitly cutting the losing broad and 'sustainable' pockets, and assumes that line jumps from 2.03 to 2.6 ROAS. The profit forecast leans on that optimism.
to10: Cut or cap the 1.2 and 1.6 ROAS themes directly, size Performance Max to what is proven above break-even, and give the first week owners and dates.

strength: It reads the data sharply and the working holds up. It explains the 2.1-day courier silence with an honest 'Packed' email, and it halves the fit-finder gain because early quiz users chose themselves, so it doesn't take the full 19 points as given.
mistake: It gives single-point targets (6,762 tickets, 28.7% bra return rate) instead of a range. It also skips a day-3 'still on track' nudge, the very days when 62% of tickets arrive.
to10: Give low and high ranges for each saving, add a short day-3 update, and put real fit tips in the post-delivery bra email.

strength: It gives honest ranges for every fix, and the maths checks out (2,430 to 3,646 fewer tickets, 540 to 1,080 fewer bra returns, £11,830 to £19,770 saved). It also adds a day-3 'nearly there' update and a delivery email for bra buyers with practical fit tips, written in our voice.
mistake: The order confirmation says 'We're packing your order now', which may not be true. The size-return portal pre-selects swap. Refund is still one tap away, but some customers could read that as nudging.
to10: Make the confirmation copy literally true, test the swap-first portal against a control instead of only using a hold-out on messages, and trim the six messages to the ones that pay their way.

strength: It brings back the pause as the main save, drops discounts entirely with a data reason, and its maths matches my numbers exactly (1,771 kept, about £15,900 a month), with an honest note that only the pause row is proven.
mistake: It gives the team no clear build order or holdout group; the launch checks are there but not sequenced.
to10: Add a short sprint build order and a small holdout on today's flow so we can prove the gain rather than assume it.

strength: Practical build notes: it puts the pause first, reads plan and reminder status on load, and holds out 10% on today's flow, which my team could start next sprint.
mistake: It keeps 50% off for switchers when that offer only holds 39% of takers, and labels the £607 as 'after discount' although it counts those people at full price.
to10: Drop the switcher discount or count it at half price for the first three months, and keep the build plan and holdout.

strength: The ticket forecast is built from your own 'Did this help?' rates and a stated reach assumption, with a low-to-high range (1,455 to 3,395 fewer tickets), so I can check it against reality after four weeks.
mistake: It puts the Simplify debts answer in a new article and only adds two link lines to 'How balances work', so the 21,000-view article that people actually land on still doesn't answer them in its first lines.
to10: Rewrite 'How balances work' itself so it opens with Simplify debts, and add the website restore steps and cancel-renewal steps to the articles.

strength: The three articles are the most complete and usable: web and app steps for restore, exact cancel-renewal paths, and a smart in-app 'Balances are simplified. Why?' line on the balance screen.
mistake: The forecast rests on avoidance shares it simply picks (40%, 50%), counts a currency article that can't be written until the conversion rules are known, and gives no high end, so the 3,700 headline looks firmer than it is.
to10: Tie the avoidance shares to the help-rate data, give a full range, and treat 'Recording a payment' as a findability problem (3,600 tickets despite 71% helpful) instead of a low-gain merge.

strength: It gives a straight 'no' to the 20% cut with correct lifetime maths and the 12.5% break-even. It also shows that cutting only new customers saves about $38,000, not the $210,000 finance expects.
mistake: Paying the top tier the same rate and relying on perks leaves some risk that top partners go to the rival paying 40%. The plan doesn't fully test that risk beyond the July review trigger.
to10: Model a fallback response if a named top-20 partner is offered 40% elsewhere, and show the extra cost of the 60/90-day windows in dollars.

strength: It shows all the numbers clearly: lifetime maths, break-even, first-year commission at 20/30/40%, and a cost for each change. It sets measurable day-90 targets, such as raising the credited share from 42% toward 70%.
mistake: It adds a 40% first-year rate for Partners and a 90-day window for everyone. That adds roughly $46,000 plus $63,000 per 10% lift in credited revenue, which pushes costs up even though the survey said payout speed was the main problem. Regular affiliates are still paid 30 days after month end with a $50 minimum.
to10: Drop or test the 40% tier, make payouts faster and the minimum lower for everyone, and put real dates on the 30-day plan.

strength: It finds the top-5 matte stock-out and fixes it with re-cartoning, a rush order and a January trigger. The sums are right (25,000 x ₹207, total ₹1,14,13,400) and the glitter clearance steps avoid fake urgency.
mistake: It leaves ₹5.87 lakh unspent and hedges with if/else rules on foundation shades and the January order, when the owner asked for one plan. It also looks over the 900-word limit.
to10: Cut it to under 900 words, take out the conditionals so it reads as one decisive plan, and put the spare cash to work.

strength: It gives one decisive plan: a rush and a standard order for the top 5 (₹1.187 crore total, all sums right), the re-carton job on Monday, and a dated action table. It shows stock at 6 Feb for every line and spells out the one-week gap honestly, with a back-in-stock line in the brand's voice and a nod to Tanvi's and Farah's words.
mistake: The cap of 4 per shade works against Farah, who buys 6 to 10 units. The "any 2 for ₹999" liquid lipstick deal is roughly 29% off, even though the text says no deep discount.
to10: Exempt pre-ordering artists from the cap, size the liquid lipstick offer to margin, and show the pre-order demand working.

strength: It takes the 4.0 ROAS apart against the 2.5 break-even with a profit-per-line table, and gives a full $240,000 split with a small $30k reserve, daily budgets, and search headlines in the brand voice.
mistake: The forecast is optimistic: 4.6 ROAS and +$61k profit rest on assumed ROAS for a brand-new Search campaign and on PMax improving from about 2.0 to 2.6 while its spend is cut. It also never tests whether removing brand from PMax hurts new-customer sales.
to10: Keep the same clear split but tie the forecast to a measured brand-exclusion check and to ROAS gates that each line must pass before it keeps its money.

strength: It is rigorous about profit: contribution per line, a cautious base case with a stated downside, Friday reserve rules with ROAS gates, a brand-exclusion test read against Shopify new-customer orders, and Black Friday timing for feed prices.
mistake: It commits only $122k and leaves $118k in a reserve, so the 30-day split is less decisive, and it invents a date range and Black Friday context the brief did not give.
to10: Commit more of the budget to proven lines up front, trim the length to fit 1,000 words, and add a few ready-to-run search headlines in the brand voice.

strength: Rigorous worked numbers that discount fit-finder users' self-selection (9.5 points, not 19) and a 50/50 portal test with a 10% holdout and a guardrail on time to refund.
mistake: It has no day-3 'still on track' update, which is the cheap fix aimed at the day 3-5 ticket spike. It gives a single point estimate for each lever, and the post-delivery fit email is generic rather than a real fit guide for first-time bra buyers.
to10: Add a day-3 reassurance message and real bra fit guidance after delivery, show low and high ranges instead of single targets, and trim it to the 1,000-word limit.

strength: It includes a day-3 'nearly there' update and a delivered email that coaches bra fit in plain words ('comfort beats the number on the tag'). Its numbers are low-to-high ranges whose working checks out.
mistake: The portal pre-selects Swap for size reasons, which is a gentle nudge that could feel like pressure, and it never says how the portal change will be tested. It also invents a 2-hour order-edit window and makes a free-switch promise from it.
to10: Make the swap first but not pre-selected, add a portal A/B test with a guardrail metric, and confirm the order-edit window rather than assuming it.

strength: It brings the pause back as the main save for 'no time' and gives a clear sprint build order, with turning the pause on first and a 10% holdout on today's flow.
mistake: It keeps a 50% discount for 'switching apps' on an unsupported 3.5% guess, and the line 'worth £607 after discount' multiplies by the full £9, which is the discounted-as-full-price error the owner dislikes.
to10: Drop the unfounded switching discount, show an honest range on the guessed rows, and add first-month signals with a stop rule.

strength: It puts the result first, with working that traces to the data: 1,771 kept from the pause, 2,172 against 842 today, +£10,734. It separates the proven pause from the guessed rows and says how to measure them, including when to drop an offer.
mistake: It runs past the 1,000-word limit and has no explicit build order for the sprint, only a confirm-before-launch checklist.
to10: Trim to 1,000 words, add a numbered build sequence and a day-30 scorecard with targets, and give the savings as a range.

strength: Honest, traceable forecast with a stated reach assumption, a 1,500 to 3,400 range, a per-topic table, and a short list of facts to confirm. The three new articles are in the brand voice and answer in the first lines.
mistake: It writes new articles beside the old ones instead of fixing the 38%-helpful 'How balances work', so the old article stays unhelpful and two similar articles now compete. It also applies one 58% help rate to every topic, including Pro refunds, where the help rate is not the right measure.
to10: Fix the existing balances article instead of adding a duplicate, and size each topic's saving on its own cause (for example, Apple and Google refunds avoided) rather than one blended help rate.

strength: It rewrites and renames the existing articles, which is the cheapest route to the ticket savings. Each topic is sized separately in a table. It also adds an in-app 'Balances are simplified. Why?' line, search-term tagging, and a currency link.
mistake: The forecast shares (40%, 50%) are asserted with little evidence and look optimistic, so the headline 21% drop is probably too high. The website steps ('Undelete expense', 'Recent activity') and the Apple and Google cancel paths are invented details, and the 'Contact us' form option is assumed.
to10: Tie the avoidance shares to the existing help rates or give a low-to-high range up front, and flag the invented UI names as needing a check.

strength: A straight no to the 20% cut, backed by the lifetime maths ($1,677 vs $1,130, net $1,174) and a per-change cost estimate for the 90-day window, the Partner tier and the payout timing.
mistake: The Partner tier adds 40% for the first 12 months and a 90-day window for everyone. That raises cost across the board when the data points to payouts and credit, and the first-30-days plan has day ranges with no dates or named owners.
to10: Keep the extra cost on the top tier, put real dates and owners on the first 30 days, and spend the perk budget on the top 20 rather than on first-customer bonuses for new affiliates.

strength: A clean maths table that says no to the cut, plus the point that the $210,000 saving would hit customers already promised 'for life'. It names what would change its mind, and it keeps the rate at 30% while fixing the payout and window complaints.
mistake: The $38,000 'new customers only' saving rests on a derived assumption of about 104 new referred customers a month. The 60-day window for ordinary members also gives less than the 90 days the data supports.
to10: Give the 90-day window to everyone and add a rough cost for the window change, so the finance lead sees the full price of the fixes.

strength: It finds that the top 5 shades run out about 30 November and fixes it with re-cartoning, a ₹207 rush order landing 7 December and a standard order. The total of ₹1,14,13,400 checks out, with ₹5.87 lakh kept as a costed buffer.
mistake: There is no forward cover view for every line, so the owner can't see where liquid lipstick, foundation and kohl stand in February. The glitter add-on is tied to lipstick orders during the window when the top shades are out of stock.
to10: Add a line-by-line stock-left-on-6-February table and a single dated action calendar for the ops lead.

strength: Every line is projected to 6 February, and the plan says re-cartoning moves the top-5 sell-out from about 23 November to 30 November. A dated Monday-to-February action table and honest back-in-stock copy in our voice ('Tanvi will wait a week, and this is a week') make it ready to run.
mistake: Only ₹1.3 lakh is left spare inside the ₹1.2 crore. The 4-per-shade cap could frustrate bridal artists who buy 6 to 10 units, unless the pro pre-order really catches them.
to10: Keep a larger cash buffer with a trigger for moving foundation or kohl to rush, and exempt verified makeup artists from the order cap.

strength: It takes the 4.0 apart against the 2.5 break-even with correct numbers: PMax without brand at 2.03, -$36,708, and total contribution of $144,960. It also gives a hands-on diagnosis of the price mismatch and turns on automatic item updates.
mistake: It keeps $128,000 in Performance Max with no negatives on the 1.2 'women's flats' or 1.6 'sustainable' pockets and simply assumes 2.6. Its own cautious case of 2.2 is below break-even, so the biggest line could still lose about $15,000.
to10: Strip the losing broad and sustainable pockets out of PMax with negatives or a much smaller budget, so even the cautious case is above 2.5 on every line.

strength: The numbers all check: $41,400 non-brand contribution in the base case, $27,400 in the downside, and a split that adds to $240,000. Every line clears break-even even in the downside. Clear Friday reserve rules, the Black Friday freeze and the discount-adjusted 4.0 break-even are things I hadn't thought through.
mistake: Committing only $122,000 gives up about $114,000 of non-brand sales. The fix for recurring price mismatches is thinner than it should be, with no automatic item updates, and the four-week staggered title rollout is slow for a 30-day plan.
to10: Add automatic item updates and a size-level price check to stop the mismatch coming back, and roll the new titles out faster on the disapproved pointed flats first.

strength: It gives honest low-to-high ranges for each fix, all checking out (2,430 to 3,646 tickets, 540 to 1,080 bra returns, £11,830 to £19,770 saved), and adds a real bra fit-check in the delivered email that could stop a return before it starts.
mistake: Measurement is thin: there is a 10% hold-out but no A/B test of the portal, no guardrail such as time to refund, and no note that returns lag orders, so a day-60 read will be misleading.
to10: Add a 50/50 portal test with a time-to-refund guardrail and a note on return lag, and rank the three fixes in one money table that includes the cost of shipping swaps.

strength: Strong measurement design: the portal runs 50/50, there is a hold-out, a time-to-refund guardrail and a return-lag caveat, and every working is shown and correct, including the self-selection haircut on the fit finder (684 fewer returns).

strength: It clearly rejects the 20% cut with the right LTV math and focuses attention on faster payouts, better attribution, and the active creator-educator partners.

strength: It reads the top-5 matte shade crisis correctly, makes the re-cartoning job the Monday task, and keeps the whole order inside ₹1.2 crore with dated actions, a useful rule for the 19 slow shades, and honest back-in-stock copy in the brand voice.

strength: Takes the 4.0 ROAS apart against the 2.5 break-even, shows PMax brand masking a 2.03 non-brand ROAS, and puts the size 5-7.5 price-mismatch feed fix first as a revenue recovery, not a budget question.

strength: Finds and names the exact signals that matter — brand masking, the half-switched-off bestseller (15.6% of site revenue), the starved bags campaign — then commits only $122,000 while releasing $118,000 on a clear Friday reserve rule, with a Black Friday discount break-even warning the brief didn't ask for but the owner needs.

strength: It fixes the three problems in the exact order the data demands (silence, then swap-first portal, then fit finder), with the money working shown for each and honest halved assumptions rather than the full 19-point fit gain.

to10: Separate cash saved from sales kept into two clearly labelled pools (and flag the swap margin unknown), so the headline number an owner repeats cannot be mistaken for profit.

strength: The copy is the best-written of the two in our voice, plain and warm with no banned words, and the delivered-fit message ('band on the loosest hook', 'comfort beats the number on the tag') is a genuinely useful post-delivery fit helper.

to10: Tie every range to a stated assumption and give one planning number per fix, as the owner asked for a number to expect, not a spread that hides the decision.

strength: It answers the owner's exact asks in order — ranked fixes, three publish-ready articles in the brand voice, the in-app links, and a transparent per-topic ticket forecast with a low-end sensitivity case.

to10: Verify the button names and restore behaviour on iPhone, Android and web before publishing, and ground the avoid-share estimates in one piece of evidence (a past article change or the 'Did this help?' change over time) rather than assertion.

strength: It is short, confident and readable, with the 'short answer' up front and a clean five-link plan, so it is quick for an owner to skim and act on.

strength: It answers the 20% question with the lifetime maths, keeps the top 20 at the centre, and turns the 30-day credit window and payout complaints into concrete fixes the one manager can run.

strength: Clear, plain-English case for holding 30% and a well-explained 90-day window, with a Partner tier that rewards the top 20 and a first 30 days anyone could run.

strength: It names the real ticket cause (the 2.1-day wait for the courier's first scan) and writes a 'Packed' email that pre-explains 'no updates yet', then shows the working behind every saving.

to10: Carry the selection-bias caveat into a low-to-high range for each fix, and send the post-delivery fit help only to first-time bra buyers.

strength: Every fix comes with an honest low-to-high range and the arithmetic, plus a delivered-bra message that actually teaches a first-time buyer how the band and cups should feel before she decides to return.

to10: Cost the SMS into the saving, apply the quiz reduction before the swap arithmetic, and keep the copy as warm and tight as the order-confirmation subject line.

strength: It follows the data straight down the line: rewrites the 21,000-view/38%-helpful balances article with Jordan's question as the heading, retitles the delete article to match the 4,900 zero-click searches, and puts the answer first in every piece.

strength: It builds the forecast from the store's own numbers (58% as the middle 'Did this help?' score) and gives a real range with 30% and 70% reach sensitivities, plus the sharp read that the payments article is 71% helpful yet still generates 3,600 tickets because people cannot find it.

strength: It nails the core signal — top-5 matte shades out ~30 Nov, re-carton the held 3,900 first, rush the top 5, skip slow lines — and lands inside ₹1.2 crore with a Monday task list and an honest back-in-stock message.

strength: It builds a date-by-date top-5 stock table (5,200 sellable → 0 ~30 Nov → rush lands 7 Dec → 2.5x sale → standard lands 28 Dec), names owners on every action, and holds ₹5.87 lakh as real buffer while giving a clear weekly check and January reorder rule.
mistake: The glitter palette clearance prices (₹899 add-on, ₹799 sale) and the 15,000-unit liquidation line are not tied to a gross-profit calc, so the 'turn it back into cash' promise is asserted rather than shown.
to10: Show the gross profit per palette under the ₹899/₹799/clearance paths (after pick-pack and marketplace fees) so the clearance decision is money-first, and tighten the back-in-stock copy to brand voice.

strength: Takes the 4.0 apart against the 2.5 break-even, puts the feed fix first, and rebuilds the $240,000 with a disciplined reserve rule that adds to exactly $240,000.

strength: Clean diagnosis of brand leaking into PMax (11% of spend, 50% of value), the 2.03 non-brand ROAS and the $36.7k loss, plus a strong feed-fix checklist with concrete root causes.

strength: It gets the three levers right, orders them by cost to fix, and writes each message in the brand's voice with one clear button.

strength: The numbers are worked line by line with the assumptions named, the fit-finder gain is honestly halved rather than taken at face value, and the guardrails (time to refund, day-60 read) show real judgement.

strength: It rebuilds the flow around the data's three signals (pause for 'no time', annual switch for monthly 'too expensive', reminder for 'not progressing') and shows the money with honest assumptions.

strength: It is disciplined: no discount anywhere, the pause is front and centre, every number traces cleanly to the brief, and it ends with a measurement plan and pre-launch confirmations the team can act on.

strength: Ranks fixes by tickets we can actually remove, gives the Simplify debts math and working, and writes all three articles answer-first in our voice.

strength: Straight no to the 20% cut with the lifetime maths shown, and the credit-window and payout fixes put first because they are cheap and fix Kwame's complaint.

strength: Names the Monday re-cartoning job and the rush order for the top 5 shades, with dates, costs and everything inside the ₹1.2 crore cash ceiling.

strength: Every number traces to the brief: total ₹1,14,13,400 with ₹5,86,600 held back, a date-by-date top-5 stock table, and an 8-week reorder point the ops lead can run every Monday.

strength: Ranks the three fixes by money saved with arithmetic that all traces back to my data and a crisp target table the team can chase.

strength: Takes the 4.0 ROAS apart against the 2.5 break-even, puts the feed fix first with the revenue math, and commits only $122,000 with a weekly reserve rule that adds to exactly $240,000.

strength: Brings back the proven pause, segments offers by reason, and shows the money cleanly, with today's 842 kept and the pause alone beating it.

strength: It nails the core decision with the lifetime-value maths, keeps 30%, and turns the broken 30-day window and slow payouts into the first fixes.

strength: Every number is shown in a plain 'how I got it' table, and it finds the $38,000 real saving versus the $210,000 headline, which is the sharpest single insight in either plan.

strength: Deep technical media buying accuracy, from diagnosing the structured data cause of the feed error to calculating the exact budget needed to close the impression share gap ($18k / 62% = $29k).
